correctness.rationale: In the full orthonormal characteristic embedding, the saturated matching with all unmatched B-vertices has q chosen coordinates, orbit mean c and common squared distance R²=q−(d²+p)/q=p(2q−p−1)/q. The orbit variance identity gives the lower bound R²+||z−c||² for every candidate center z. Any total matching with k edges uses extra vertices from at most one side, and under d(p−d)≥2p the coefficients of vertex support are both positive. For maximum support the squared distances from c are H+p−2k/q for side A and H+p−d+2k(d−1)/q for side B, with H=(d²+p)/q. The former decreases and the latter increases strictly, whose extreme difference is (d(p−d)−2p)/q. This proves optimality and exhausts contacts, including the unique all-A vector at equality. Necessity follows because a minimum-ball center belongs to the convex hull of its contacts (moving toward its projection onto that hull decreases all active distances and preserves slack for the rest); its symmetry then makes it the orbit mean if that orbit is the sole contact set. The all-A vector consequently forces the strict inequality. The equality equation gives p=d+2+4/(d−2), so d−2=1,2,4, and strictness gives the claimed integer intervals by the concave quadratic and the endpoints d=2,3,p−3,p−2, checking p=9 separately. The supplied finite calculation was inspected, not executed; the proof uses no grid extrapolation.

value.rationale: An exact criterion tells when a single natural symmetry orbit certifies the circumradius despite the presence of both edge and vertex coordinates. The proof identifies the all-A vector as the only competitor at the boundary, including the three integral ties. This is a useful sharp screening invariant of a standard polytope family, rather than a dimension-specific computation or a claim to solve the radius outside the screened range.
